cards.title: Sublinear-round clique detection in CONGEST
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved affirmatively: for every fixed integer p≥4, can an n-node network detect a copy of Kₚ in o(n) synchronous CONGEST rounds, with success probability at least 2/3 on every input graph? In particular, can K₄ be detected in sublinear rounds? The later listing theorem gives Õ(n^{1−2/p}) rounds and therefore answers both questions. For p=4, the resulting Õ(√n) bound matches the original Ω(√n/log n) detection lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors.
cards.why: Locates the bandwidth cost of finding a basic dense pattern when processors communicate only along the input graph. The historical K₄ case now has matching upper and lower exponents; the broader fixed-clique sublinearity question is also answered.
cards.status_note: Read the original local detection convention and concluding K₄ question. Matched the SODA 2021 CONGEST listing theorem to that task and checked the later PODC 2022 deterministic theorem in their full preprints and publication records. The resolution is for each fixed p; it does not give a uniform sublinear guarantee for growing clique size or classify detection for every p via listing lower bounds. No independent proof audit.

progress.text: Source proves the K₄ detection lower bound Ω(√n/log n) and asks whether sublinear detection is possible.
SODA Theorem 1.1 gives randomized listing in Õ(n^{1−2/p}) rounds for each fixed p≥4, resolving the historical question and matching K₄ detection up to polylogarithmic factors.
PODC Theorem 1 gives deterministic listing in n^{1−2/p+o(1)} rounds for every fixed p≥3.

references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 14; PDF page 14

cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph G=(V,E), |V|=n. Each vertex is a processor and each edge is a bidirectional communication link. Initially a node knows n, the fixed p, its own unique identifier and its neighbors’ identifiers; identifiers use O(log₂(n+2)) bits. The same algorithm is used at all nodes, with these local inputs, and for all graph sizes. Each round permits unlimited local computation and one O(log₂(n+2))-bit message in each direction on each incident edge; different edges may carry different messages. There is no direct communication between nonadjacent nodes. The protocol may use independent private random bits. Time counts synchronous rounds, not local computation, output length or aggregate messages. Each node outputs a bit. If G contains p distinct pairwise adjacent vertices, at least one node must output 1 with probability at least 2/3; otherwise all nodes must output 0 with probability at least 2/3. No designated node or every-node global verdict is required. The probability is over all algorithmic coins for the fixed graph and identifiers. Disconnected graphs are allowed. The round bound can be taken as a deterministic cutoff, counting overruns as failure. A sublinear bound Tₚ(n) satisfies Tₚ(n)/n→0 as n→∞ with p fixed. Õ suppresses a fixed power of log(n+2), with constants allowed to depend on p. Listing means every Kₚ is output as a tuple of identifiers by at least one node, with no false tuples; a node need not belong to the clique it outputs. Such listing implies the required local detection. The fixed-p limit is essential: no bound uniformly sublinear for p growing with n is asserted.
cards.answer_criterion: The affirmative resolution supplies the local detection algorithm and proves its success and o(n) round bound for each fixed p≥4. The SODA 2021 theorem solves the stronger listing task in Õ(n^{1−2/p}) rounds with high probability. Its p=4 case also gives a matching detection classification up to polylogarithmic factors. Listing lower bounds for p>4 are not automatically lower bounds for detection.

context_blocks.title: The original gap concerned communication
context_blocks.text: The 2018 paper gave a nontrivial lower bound but left a gap to the linear-round upper bound. Its conclusion singled out K₄ as a test case for whether even fixed-size clique detection might require nearly linear communication rounds.

context_blocks.title: A later theorem closes the sublinearity question
context_blocks.text: The SODA 2021 result lists every fixed-size clique in Õ(n^{1−2/p}) rounds in CONGEST itself. Since some node learns each clique, this gives the detection output required by the original paper without a network-wide announcement.

context_blocks.title: Randomness is not needed for sublinearity
context_blocks.text: PODC 2022 gives deterministic listing in n^{1−2/p+o(1)} rounds for every fixed p≥3. This also yields sublinear deterministic detection. Its n^{o(1)} overhead is a different precision from the randomized polylogarithmic overhead.

context_blocks.title: The stronger communication model is separate
context_blocks.text: The congested-clique model permits every pair of nodes to communicate directly each round. The resolving upper bound operates on the actual edges of G in CONGEST. Equality of listing complexities between these models is an additional result, not an assumption used to reinterpret this card.

cards.title: Private randomness in algorithmic secret-key agreement
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Historical question, answered by the 2020 follow-up and its expanded 2024 version: does the worst-case communication barrier min{C(x|y),C(y|x)}−O(log n) for secret-key agreement persist when Alice and Bob use independent private random bits? The answer is affirmative for the bounded-error secret-key task below. In particular, on a hard family of pairs of n-bit inputs with C(x|y), C(y|x) and I(x:y) all equal to n/2 within O(log n), every uniformly computable protocol that succeeds on the promised inputs with probability greater than 1/2 has worst-case communication at least n/2−O(log n). This holds even for a secret key of length δ(n)=ω(log n), instead of the maximal length I(x:y)−O(log n). The follow-up explicitly identifies this as its answer to the source’s Open Question 1.
cards.why: Establishes that hidden local randomness cannot remove the worst-case communication needed to turn algorithmic correlation into a shared secret. This isolates communication as a resource distinct from computational hardness and from the amount of mutual information.
cards.status_note: Read the original conference and full 2019 formulations, the MFCS 2020 theorem, and the expanded May 2024 text’s Theorem 2, Proposition 1, model and conclusion. Matched the private-coin setting, supplied complexity profile, secrecy, uniformity, worst-case cost and removal of the randomness cap. The later authors explicitly state that they answer the cited open question. The displayed later theorem uses success greater than 1/2; no literal all-parameter extension of the original theorem’s arbitrary-positive-success phrasing is claimed here. Checked the journal’s actual September 2024 publication dates via publisher-deposited metadata and the author’s current publication list. No independent proof audit.

cards.definitions: Fix an optimal plain universal description machine U and a computable encoding of tuples. C(x|y) is the minimum bit length of a program p with U(p,y)=x; C(x)=C(x|empty string), C(x,y)=C(⟨x,y⟩), and I(x:y)=C(x)+C(y)−C(x,y). Alice receives x∈{0,1}ⁿ and Bob receives y∈{0,1}ⁿ. Both additionally receive the exact complexity profile p=(C(x),C(y),C(x,y)); the profile and the fixed protocol are public. This small auxiliary input is supplied, not computed from x or y. The parties use independent fair private coin sequences, independent of the fixed input pair. They exchange messages on a public noiseless channel, then separately output strings z_A,z_B. The transcript t records all publicly communicated bits and their order; actual transmitted framing is charged too. Cost is the worst-case total number of communicated bits over legal inputs and coin outcomes, not its expectation. The same finite algorithms compute messages and outputs for all n. Local computation and the number of interaction rounds have no polynomial bound; the protocol must terminate on every input and coin outcome, even for invalid auxiliary profiles, where output correctness is not required. The expanded result permits any finite number of private random bits, without a polynomial bound in n. Success means z_A=z_B=z of the requested length and C(z|t,p)≥|z|−O(log n), so agreement on a public string does not qualify as secrecy. Probability is over the private coins, separately for each promised input pair; x,y need not come from an independent, identically distributed or computable source. The hard-family profile equalities and lower bound mean additive deviations bounded by fixed multiples of log₂(n+2) for sufficiently large n; these constants can depend on U and the fixed protocol, not on n or its coin outcomes. The notation δ(n)=ω(log n) means δ(n)/log₂(n+2)→∞. Only attainable secret-key lengths are relevant; the maximal length is I(x:y) up to logarithmic terms.
cards.answer_criterion: The historical communication-barrier question is settled for bounded-error secret-key agreement by the follow-up’s Theorem 2, together with the earlier matching upper bound. The recorded quantitative theorem has success probability greater than 1/2 and incompressible secret keys. The original Theorem 7 was phrased more generally using arbitrary positive constant success probability and a lower bound directly on conditional key complexity; this review does not claim that the follow-up’s displayed theorem reproduces every such parameter verbatim. It records the follow-up’s explicit resolution of the usual secret-key task and its precise scope.

context_blocks.title: Mutual information is achievable as a secret key
context_blocks.text: The original paper gives a protocol producing a shared secret of length I(x:y) within logarithmic precision using min{C(x|y),C(y|x)}+O(log n) communication. Both parties know the complexity profile. The unresolved issue in the extracted passage was the matching communication lower bound with private coins, not the achievable key length.

context_blocks.title: Private coins require a separate lower bound
context_blocks.text: In the public-coin model the eavesdropper sees the random string as well as the communication, so secrecy is conditioned on both. Private coins are hidden unless communicated. They cannot simply be declared public without changing the secrecy requirement.

context_blocks.title: The later result answers the cited question
context_blocks.text: The MFCS 2020 introduction explicitly points to the earlier Open Question 1 and gives an affirmative answer. Its Theorem 2 shows a sharp worst-case threshold even when only a superlogarithmic secret key is requested, initially with polynomially many private random bits.

context_blocks.title: The unrestricted-randomness version is later
context_blocks.text: The expanded 2024 text removes that randomness restriction and supplies full proofs. The bound concerns worst-case input pairs: the same paper exhibits other pairs with similar complexity profiles for which shorter secret keys need less communication. A lower bound for every individual pair is not asserted.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.
